title: Can we identify young people and adults who may benefit from methylphenidate, the most common medication for ADHD, from their initial response to a single test dose rather than after several weeks of daily treatment?
official: The first test dose to predict longer-term treatment response in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: Combined Approach to Response Evaluation in ADHD v.1 (CARE-ADHD)
summary:
Background and study aims
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is very common, and people with ADHD often wait years to start treatment. Once they start, it can take months to find the right medication for them. Stimulant medications, such as methylphenidate (MPH), are generally effective, but response may vary from person to person. MPH is often given first, and patients need to take it every day for several weeks before a clinician can tell if it is right for them. If MPH does not work, clinicians will try other medicines, one by one. This approach is expensive and delays getting the right treatment. Without the right treatment, people with ADHD have higher chances to do poorly in school or work. With this study, we want to understand if MPH is the right medicine for a person with ADHD or if they need another one faster. 

Who can participate?
We are currently recruiting young people and adults (aged 12 to 64 years) from existing ADHD waiting lists at participating NHS Trusts only (Hampshire and Isle of Wight Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust and South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust). 
IMPORTANT: Please note that we will not be able to recruit participants from other NHS Trusts or via any website.

What does the study involve?
Participants will complete clinical questionnaires, cognitive tasks measuring skills such as attention, and physiological measures such as pulse under MPH and under placebo over two separate days. They will then start standard treatment with MPH. We will follow them up at 2 and 6 months.   

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Eligible participants will be started on standard ADHD treatment. Since there are currently very long waiting lists for ADHD treatment, this might mean that participants could start treatment earlier. 
During the initial two-month treatment with MPH, our research team will also provide regular check-ins (e.g., via phone call) additional to standard care to see how participants are doing. 
Participating in this study will improve our understanding of ADHD treatment. While it may not bring participants a direct clinical benefit, this may help improve care for other people with ADHD in the future.
Those who choose to participate in this study will be compensated for their time. They will receive £50 at the completion of the 2-month follow-up and £30 at the completion of the 6-month follow-up. Travel expenses for the two experimental visits will be reimbursed up to £20 per participant.
Medication for ADHD, including the initial dose administered when we do the tests, could have side effects. These are usually mild, like headaches, stomach aches, and mild increases in pulse and blood pressure. To reduce risks, medication will be prescribed and monitored by one of our NHS clinicians. During the study, participants will be asked to swallow small capsules. Therefore, we will ask participants if they can safely swallow small capsules.  

Where is the study run from?
University of Southampton (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
August 2026 to August 2028

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Valeria Parlatini
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age >=12 and <=64 years
2. Clinical diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) confirmed according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5-TR). Participants will be mainly recruited from treatment waiting lists but new referrals will also be invited, and assessments carried out as per standard practice and according to DSM-5-TR criteria
3. No prior treatment with methylphenidate (MPH) for at least 1 year
4. Willing to start treatment with MPH
5. Participants will be included only if they (or their parents, if participant is below 16 years old) have capacity to give informed consent, in addition to assent if participant is below 16 years old
6. Able to swallow small capsules (single dose testing)
7. Able to complete the computer-based tasks used in this study
8. Currently on waiting list for starting ADHD treatment (or assessment and treatment)
Exclusion criteria:
1. No conditions for which MPH or participation would be considered inappropriate according to the treating clinician (e.g., contraindications to treatment or crisis presentations)
2. No concurrent pregnancy or pregnancy-planning or lactation
3. No concurrent psychopharmacological treatment, except for melatonin, promethazine and sleeping tablets to avoid confounding during single-dose testing
4. Individuals not able to understand and follow instructions to complete the computer-based and other tasks involved in this study and/or to provide valid consent/assent
